lead: A liquid cooling loop moves heat from the engine jacket to the radiator. It can run on density difference alone (thermosyphon), on a pump (forced circulation), or under a pressure cap that lifts the boiling point. The coolant—water or a glycol mix—sets the safe upper temperature. Only a few universities teach all three arrangements at full depth. Road engines use forced circulation with a pressure cap; thermosyphon survives on small stationary engines.
prereq: You need: the jacket, pump, radiator and thermostat from Need for cooling; air and liquid cooling systems, and saturation temperature from thermodynamics.

blocks.text: Hot water is lighter than cold water. In a closed loop, the column from the jacket to the radiator is hot and light; the downcomer is cold and heavy. Gravity pulls the heavy column down and pushes the light column up. Flow continues without a pump.

blocks.where: Δp is the driving pressure in Pa; ρ<sub>c</sub> is cold-water density in kg/m³; ρ<sub>h</sub> is hot-water density in kg/m³; g is 9.81 m/s²; h is the height between jacket centre and radiator centre in m.

blocks.text: The head is small, tens of pascals in a car-sized loop, so pipes are short and wide and the radiator sits well above the engine. Flow only starts once the water is hot, and it rises with the temperature difference. A small stationary engine at steady load copes; a vehicle engine at high load needs a pump.

A pump, usually belt-driven from the crankshaft, pushes coolant through the jacket, radiator and heater. A thermostat blocks flow to the radiator until the coolant reaches about 80–90 °C, then opens; a bypass route keeps the pump circulating during warm-up. An expansion tank gives the coolant room to expand and keeps the pump inlet flooded. Forced circulation gives a predictable flow at all speeds, so the radiator can be smaller.

A pressure cap is a spring-loaded valve. It holds the system above atmospheric pressure and raises the boiling point, because saturation temperature rises with pressure: a cap set 100 kPa above atmosphere lifts the boiling point of water from 100 °C to about 120 °C. The cap removes no heat itself. What it buys is margin: the coolant can run hotter without boiling, the larger coolant-to-air temperature difference lets a smaller radiator reject the same heat, and the system does not boil away on a hill climb or at altitude. The cap holds two valves: the pressure valve opens to the overflow tank when the set pressure is passed, and a small vacuum valve lets coolant flow back as the engine cools. Never open a hot cap: the sudden drop to atmospheric pressure flashes coolant to steam and scalds. A faulty cap lets the engine boil at a lower temperature;

A good coolant has a high specific heat and thermal conductivity, a low freezing point, a high boiling point, low viscosity so the pump moves it easily, no attack on iron, aluminium, copper and rubber hoses, no foaming, chemical stability over long service, and low cost and toxicity. Water has the best specific heat (about 4.18 kJ/kg·K) and is cheap, but it freezes at 0 °C, corrodes iron and aluminium, and hard water leaves calcium and magnesium scale on hot walls. Scale insulates and can block narrow passages.

Ethylene glycol (EG) and propylene glycol (PG) lower the freezing point and raise the boiling point. A 50 percent glycol mix is common: it gives freeze protection near −37 °C (EG) and a few degrees more boiling margin, while its specific heat, roughly 3.3 to 3.6 kJ/kg·K, stays acceptable. Above about 60–70 percent glycol, freeze protection worsens and heat transfer falls. Corrosion inhibitors—silicates, phosphates, borates or organic acids—protect metals; they are consumed over time, so coolant has a service life. Use soft or distilled water with glycol concentrate, not hard tap water.

figure.caption: The thermosyphon loop of the first worked example. Hot water at 80 °C rises from the jacket to the radiator top tank, and water cooled to 40 °C falls back; the 20.4 kg/m³ density difference over 0.4 m gives only 80 Pa of driving pressure. The pressure cap lifts the boiling point to 120.4 °C.

spec.aria: A cooling loop with the engine jacket low on the left and the radiator high on the right. A riser carries 80 degree water up to the top tank; a downcomer returns 40 degree water to the jacket. The height between centres is 0.4 metres and the driving pressure is 80 pascals.

examples.question: A thermosyphon system has 0.4 m between jacket centre and radiator centre. The hot riser carries water at 80 °C and the cold downcomer water at 40 °C. Take the densities from the water tables, 971.8 kg/m³ at 80 °C and 992.2 kg/m³ at 40 °C, and g = 9.81 m/s². Find the driving pressure. Explain why a pump is added on the same engine at higher load.
steps: Identify h = 0.4 m, ρ<sub>c</sub> = 992.2 kg/m³ (40 °C), ρ<sub>h</sub> = 971.8 kg/m³ (80 °C), g = 9.81 m/s².

For comparison, 80 Pa is the pressure of an 8 mm column of water. It can push only a gentle flow through wide pipes. At higher load the heat to be removed rises, the flow needed by Q = ṁ c ΔT rises with it, and a pump that adds tens of kPa becomes necessary.
examples.answer: Δp ≈ 80 Pa, about 8 mm of water head, which is why thermosyphon loops need tall radiators and wide pipes.

examples.question: A radiator cap opens at 100 kPa gauge. Using the water tables, find the boiling point of the coolant (taken as water) (a) with the cap, at sea level where the air is at 101.3 kPa; (b) with an open system (no cap) at a hill town 2000 m up where the air is at 79.5 kPa; (c) with the same cap at that town.
steps: A cap gauge setting adds to the local atmospheric pressure: p<sub>abs</sub> = p<sub>atm</sub> + p<sub>cap</sub>.
(a) p = 101.3 + 100 = 201.3 kPa. The saturation temperature at 201.3 kPa is 120.4 °C.
(b) p = 79.5 kPa. The saturation temperature at 79.5 kPa is 93.3 °C, so an open system would boil with a 90 °C thermostat barely open.
(c) p = 79.5 + 100 = 179.5 kPa. The saturation temperature is 116.8 °C, still about 20 K above a 95 °C running temperature.
examples.answer: (a) 120.4 °C; (b) 93.3 °C; (c) 116.8 °C. The cap keeps a safe boiling margin even at altitude.

traps: A pressure cap raises the boiling point; it does not remove heat itself. The radiator gets smaller only because the hotter coolant gives a larger temperature difference to the air.
Thermosyphon flow needs height and a density difference. A horizontal loop or zero temperature difference gives no flow.
Hard water scale insulates hot walls and blocks passages; do not treat it as harmless water.
More glycol is not always better. Above about 60–70 percent, freeze protection worsens and heat transfer falls.
Opening a hot pressure cap causes flash steam and scalds; wait for the engine to cool.

quiz.q: What drives coolant flow in a thermosyphon system?
quiz.a: The density difference between hot and cold water columns, helped by height h.

quiz.q: Why does a thermostat have a bypass route?
quiz.a: During warm-up the thermostat blocks the radiator. The bypass keeps coolant moving through the jacket so the engine heats evenly and the pump does not dead-head.

quiz.q: A thermosyphon loop has h = 0.5 m, cold water at 30 °C (995.6 kg/m³) and hot water at 70 °C (977.8 kg/m³). Take g = 9.81 m/s². Find Δp.
A car boils with a new pressure cap but not with the old cap. Give the likely cause and effect.
quiz.a: The new cap has a weak spring or a bad seal, so it opens below its rated pressure. The system pressure, and with it the boiling point, is lower, so the coolant boils at a temperature the old cap held safely. Fit a cap of the correct rating.

quiz.q: Name the two common glycol coolants.
Why is a 50 percent glycol mix common instead of 100 percent glycol?
quiz.a: It gives useful freeze and boil protection while keeping heat capacity and viscosity acceptable. Stronger mixes transfer heat less well and can worsen freeze protection.

quiz.q: Why does hard water damage a cooling system even if it never freezes?
quiz.a: Calcium and magnesium salts form scale on hot surfaces. Scale insulates, reduces heat transfer, and can block narrow passages.

beyond: Production cooling systems now use electric pumps and map-controlled thermostats that change the coolant temperature with load. Coolant chemistry is a field of its own: organic acid and hybrid inhibitor packages are named in service manuals. Search terms: map-controlled thermostat, coolant inhibitor technology, saturation temperature of glycol mixtures.
